food.text: The Dnieper–Donets people were originally hunter-gatherers who lived on aurochs, elk, red deer, roe, wild boar, fox, wildcat, hare, bear and onager. Their diet was primarily high in protein, with meat, fish and nuts on the menu.

Cucuteni–Trypillia people built some of the largest settlements in Eurasia, some holding as many as three thousand structures and possibly 20,000 to 46,000 people. Because these settlements were so large, feeding them depended on agriculture.

Stable isotope ratios of Yamnaya individuals from the Dnieper Valley suggest a diet based on land-animal protein, with insignificant contribution from freshwater or aquatic resources. Anthony speculates they ate meat, milk, yogurt, cheese, and soups made from seeds and wild vegetables, and probably drank mead.

Genetic studies have shown that all modern domestic horses were exclusively domesticated in the Pontic–Caspian steppe of Eastern Europe. Earlier work had pointed to Central Asia, and horses in Paleolithic cave art were probably hunted for meat.

From around 5200 BC, the Dnieper–Donets people began keeping cattle, sheep and goats, along with pigs, horses and dogs. Over the following centuries, domestic animals from the Dnieper appeared further and further east, reaching the Volga-Ural steppes around 4700 to 4600 BC.
The Yamnaya economy was based on animal husbandry, fishing and foraging. Some agriculture was practiced near rivers, and the largest of their few fortified sites was Mikhailovka.

The Comb Ceramic culture is one of the few exceptions to the rule that pottery and farming coexist in Europe. Its bearers mostly followed a hunter-gatherer lifestyle, with only traces of early agriculture.

One theory blames the fall of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture on a dramatic climate change around 3200 BCE that brought a devastating Dust Bowl drought. With their reliance on agriculture, feeding the inhabitants of the large settlements would have become unsustainable. Pastoral nomads of the Proto-Indo-Europeans followed.
Comb Ceramic settlements sat at sea shores or beside lakes, and the economy rested on hunting, fishing and gathering plants. In Finland, the culture became more and more specialized in hunting seals.

The Cucuteni–Trypillia people supplemented their diet by hunting, killing prey with traps as well as weapons including the bow and arrow, the spear and clubs. To help them stalk game, they sometimes disguised themselves with camouflage. Remains of the animals they hunted at their sites include red deer, roe deer, aurochs, wild boar, fox and brown bear.

One theory blames a worldwide climate change around 3200 BCE for the end of the Cucuteni–Trypillia settlements. A Dust Bowl drought would have made feeding the inhabitants of these large, agriculture-reliant settlements unsustainable, and drought-suited pastoral nomads replaced them.

Domestic plants recovered from Dnieper–Donets sites include millet, wheat and pea. Yet recent evidence suggests millet did not reach west Eurasia until the Bronze Age, and systematic evidence of food production in the culture is currently lacking.

art.text: The Trypillian culture, centred in the forest-steppe zone of central Ukraine, is renowned for its ceramic artistry. Its excavated pottery vessels show meticulous craftsmanship, harmonious proportions, and geometric ornamentation rendered with natural pigments. The culture is dated to about 5400 to 2700 BCE.

The Volosovo culture, described as forest foragers, emerged sometime between the third and fourth millennium BC. Its people first used stone and bone tools and were particularly adept at bone carving and sculpture.

Scholarly study of Trypillian ceramics has helped reframe how prehistoric art is understood. Rather than an isolated or naive expression, it is seen as a complex and contextually rich visual culture. The Trypillian culture's pottery testifies to a high degree of technical skill and aesthetic complexity.

Trypillian ceramics are often interpreted as having symbolic or ritual significance. They reflect a sophisticated visual language that went beyond everyday use. This suggests that art was woven into social and cosmological life very early on.

The Volosovo culture developed a small art that has been considered rich and diverse. It included varied flaked flint sculptures representing the human form. This phenomenon was distinguished from what appeared in the Tokareva culture.

The artifacts that define the Volosovo culture came from semi-subterranean dwellings, often situated in river floors and within the area of lakes. The lower layer shows an affinity with the Pit-marked Pottery culture called Balakhna. The upper layer, the actual Volosovo phase, held ceramics distinct from pit-marked pottery.

The earliest anthropomorphic stone stelae date to the 4th millennium BC and are associated with the Yamna Horizon, especially the Kemi Oba culture of Crimea. Those in Ukraine number around three hundred, mostly crude slabs with a schematic head. About twenty more complex statue menhirs show ornaments, weapons and human or animal figures.

Experts identify a Volosovo-Garino cultural province, characterized by a distinct comb-ware ceramic tradition. The Garino-Bor culture and the Netted Ware culture are considered offshoots of the Volosovo culture that settled in the Volga-Oka region.

war.text: On the Pontic–Caspian steppe, people raised burial mounds called kurgans over graves that often held a single human body along with grave vessels, weapons and horses. Elite kurgans could also hold sacrificed animals. Berel Kurgan 11 had thirteen harnessed horses buried beside the funeral chamber, and the seventh-century BCE Kostromskaya kurgan had twenty-two horses buried in pairs around the principal grave. The tradition later spread into much of Central Asia and Eastern, Southeast, Western and Northern Europe during the third millennium BC.

In Marija Gimbutas's Kurgan hypothesis, nomadic pastoralists of the steppe expanded over the Pontic–Caspian region and into Eastern Europe by the early 3rd millennium BC. Their mobility is attributed to the domestication of the horse, followed by the use of early chariots.

In the middle Volga region, the Khvalynsk culture made stone weapons and implements of a quality that reached a high point. Its graves held metal rings and spiral metal rings, but there is no sign they were used for anything beyond ornament.

The Krivoluchie grave of the Khvalynsk culture, which Gimbutas viewed as that of a chief, contained a long flint dagger and tanged arrowheads, all carefully retouched on both faces. It also held a porphyry axe-head with lugs and a haft hole, types that not long after appeared in metal.

science.text: Around 4800 to 4400 BCE, horse bones and carved images of horses began appearing in graves of the early Khvalynsk and Samara cultures in the middle Volga region of Russia. This is the oldest possible archaeological sign of a changed relationship between horses and humans.

Talianki in Ukraine, around 3700 BCE, was the largest Trypillia settlement of its time. It held up to 2,700 houses and up to 21,000 inhabitants across 450 hectares, and regular excavations began there in 1981.

The Yamnaya culture was discovered by Vasily Gorodtsov during excavations near the Donets River in 1901 to 1903. Its name comes from the Russian word for 'related to pits', because its people buried their dead in kurgans containing simple pit chambers.

The first strong archaeological evidence for the domestication of the horse comes from the Sredny Stog culture, north of the Azov Sea in Ukraine. It would correspond to an early Proto-Indo-European or pre-Proto-Indo-European nucleus of the 5th millennium BC.

At the Khvalynsk cemetery, 26 of 201 recorded graves contained parts of sacrificed domestic animals, and more sacrifices were made in ritual deposits on the ground surface above the graves. At least 106 domesticated sheep or goats, 29 domesticated cattle and 16 horses were sacrificed there. Ten graves held parts of lower horse legs. Because horses were sacrificed alongside cattle and sheep while obviously wild animals were excluded, researchers think horses were symbolically grouped with domesticated animals.

In 2009 a British-Ukrainian expedition organized by John Chapman and Mykhailo Videiko studied the 300-hectare mega-site of Nebelivka. They produced a 15-hectare geophysics plot showing over 50 burnt structures, and excavated the remains of one house.

One theory blames the collapse of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture on a dramatic climate change around 3200 BCE, which would have brought a devastating Dust Bowl drought. Feeding such large farming settlements would have become unsustainable, and pastoral nomads later replaced the farmers.

In 2022, genetic research found the Yamnaya to be a mixture of Eastern Hunter-Gatherers, Caucasus hunter-gatherers, and Anatolian and Levantine Neolithic farmers. The admixture occurred around 4000 BCE, between a Sredny Stog-like population and a Caucasus-like population.

A stallion from the Ukrainian settlement of Dereivka, dated about 4000 BCE, had bit-related wear on its teeth. But radiocarbon dating of one worn tooth gave 700 to 200 BCE, showing the stallion was actually buried in a pit dug into the older site during the Iron Age.

politics.text: Between about 4100 and 3500 BC, the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture built some of the largest settlements in Eurasia. Some contained as many as three thousand structures and were possibly home to 20,000 to 46,000 people. These 'mega-sites' have been claimed to be early forms of cities.

Trypillian settlements were primarily administrative, military and religious centres rather than craft centres. The typical pattern was one dominant 'capital' of up to 15,000 people, surrounded by satellite towns of 10 to 40 hectares and villages of 2 to 7 hectares. The capital controlled territory as far as 20 km from its center.

The Yamnaya culture of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, dated 3300 to 2600 BC, was organised in a chiefdom system. Its people buried their dead in kurgans, tumuli containing simple pit chambers. The name comes from the Russian word yamnaya, meaning 'related to pits'.

It has been proposed that the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture was initially egalitarian, and that the rise of inequality contributed to its downfall. How it ended is debated. Marija Gimbutas argued that Kurgan invaders destroyed it by force, a theory said to find support in frequent evidence of violent death in Verteba cave. Others point to a drought that began around 3200 BC, or, as J. P. Mallory argued, to refugees abandoning 600–700 settlements in a gradual transformation. The culture's population at its peak may have reached or exceeded one million people.

Starting in 4300 BCE, the mega settlements of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture lasted for almost 2000 years. By 2014, more than 2440 settlements had been discovered in Moldova, Ukraine and Romania. Of these, 194 covered more than 10 hectares.

One theory blames the collapse of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture on climate. Around 3200 BCE, a dramatic worldwide climate change would have brought a devastating Dust Bowl drought. Feeding the large settlements would have become unsustainable, and the farmers were replaced by pastoral nomads.

The Sredny Stog culture ended around 3500 BC, when the Yamnaya culture expanded westward and replaced it. This brought the Yamnaya into direct contact with the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture in western Ukraine.

The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture built some of the largest settlements in Eurasia between about 4100 and 3500 BC, some with as many as three thousand structures. It has been proposed that the culture was initially egalitarian and that the rise of inequality contributed to its downfall. Marija Gimbutas argued that it was destroyed by force in Kurgan invasions, and frequent evidence of violent death has been found in Verteba cave. J. P. Mallory instead described refugees abandoning 600–700 settlements for caves, islands and hilltops.

A 2009 British-Ukrainian expedition organized by John Chapman and Mykhailo Videiko focused on the 300-hectare mega-site of Nebelivka. Dated to the B II period of the Trypillia culture, it was the largest settlement around 4000 BCE. Researchers mapped a 15-hectare plot showing over 50 burnt structures.

culture.text: The Samara culture of the Volga is characterised by the remains of animal sacrifice, found at most of its sites. The heads and hooves of sacrificed cattle, sheep and horses were placed in shallow bowls over a human grave and smothered with ochre. The article adds that the Indo-Europeans, like many other cultures, are known to have sacrificed both animals and people.

Settlements of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture were burned and rebuilt every 60–80 years. Some scholars think the inhabitants saw each house as a nearly living entity, sharing one circle of life with everything in it. The whole settlement may have been seen as having a life cycle of death and rebirth.

The Yamnaya culture takes its name from its burial tradition: Yamnaya is a Russian adjective meaning 'related to pits', because these people buried their dead in tumuli, or kurgans, containing simple pit chambers. The bodies were laid on their backs with knees bent and covered in ochre, and graves were often accompanied by animal offerings. Kurgan burials may have been rare and perhaps were reserved for special adults, who were predominantly male. The culture dates to 3300–2600 BC on the Pontic–Caspian steppe.

The Samara culture at the Samara Bend of the Volga has horse burials, the earliest in the Old World, though there is no indisputable evidence of riding. Graves had an overburden of horse remains, and the horses were certainly used as a meat animal. Some have seen the beginning of horse sacrifice in these remains, but that interpretation has not been firmly substantiated.

The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture left many clay figurines, which archaeologists see as akin to fetishes or totems believed to protect the people who cared for them. They are popularly but inaccurately called "goddesses". They have become a recognizable visual marker of the culture.

culture.text: Special communal sanctuary buildings began to appear in Cucuteni–Trypillia settlements in the Precucuteni III period, c. 4800–4600 BC. Their architecture was monumental, and inside were stelae, statues and shrines, sometimes packed in straw inside pottery. The sanctuaries began to disappear after about 3800 BC.
culture.source_title: Religion and ritual of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture

culture.text: The Yamnaya economy was based on animal husbandry, fishing, foraging, and making ceramics, tools and weapons. The people were nomads or semi-nomads, with some agriculture near rivers. Mikhailovka was the largest of a few fortified sites.

The Volosovo people of the Volga-Ural forest steppes have been described as forest foragers. They were particularly adept at bone carving and sculpture. Their varied flaked flint sculptures of the human form show a rich and diverse small art.
Talianki in Ukraine was the largest Trypillia settlement around 3700 BCE, with up to 21,000 inhabitants and up to 2,700 houses. It covered 450 hectares.

The Steppe theory holds that a Kurgan culture in the Pontic steppe north of the Black Sea most likely spoke Proto-Indo-European. Marija Gimbutas systematized it in the 1950s, defining four successive periods of Kurgan culture. Its earliest period, Kurgan I, included the Samara and Seroglazovka cultures.

Vasily Gorodtsov discovered the Yamnaya culture during his archaeological excavations near the Donets River in 1901–1903. Recent research suggests that Mikhailovka, on the lower Dnieper River in Ukraine, formed the core Yamnaya culture around 3600–3400 BC.

At the Khvalynsk cemetery on the middle Volga, at least 106 domesticated sheep or goats, 29 domesticated cattle, and 16 horses were sacrificed, and parts of the animals were laid in 26 of the 201 recorded graves. Ten graves held parts of lower horse legs, two of them with the bones of cattle and sheep as well. Horses were included with cattle and sheep while obviously wild animals were excluded, suggesting horses were categorized symbolically with domesticated animals.

In the Precucuteni III period, around 4800 to 4600 BC, special communal sanctuary buildings began to appear in Cucuteni–Trypillia settlements. Their architecture was monumental, and they held stelae, statues and shrines. The sanctuaries began to disappear in the Cucuteni B period, c. 3800 to 3500 BC.

culture.text: Archaeologist Valentin Sedov argued that river names ending in -sha and -xa originated in the Volosovo culture. They are found on the right bank of the Oka and around the White and Barents Seas. It is also speculated that the Volosovo people had contact with Proto-Baltic speakers in Finland and Russian Karelia.
